claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayers under sustained loading is governed primarily by interface-mediated dislocation activity.
The relevant interface-mediated activity consists of dislocation nucleation and glide at and across heterophase interfaces.
Bulk dislocation motion within the individual layers is not the primary deformation mechanism.
High compositional complexity and lattice distortion in HEAs increase resistance to dislocation motion within each phase.
The increased intralayer resistance makes interfaces the dominant plasticity pathways.
Creep is more sensitive to interface structure and chemistry than to the intrinsic properties of the constituent bulk phases.
Sustained constant-stress loading at elevated temperature can activate creep while preserving the multilayer structure if temperature and stress are appropriately selected.
Interface coherency, intermixing, and local short-range order are structural mediators of the deformation response.
FCC/BCC interfaces are preferential sites for dislocation nucleation and glide because dislocation motion faces high resistance within the distorted HEA layers.
Local atomic disorder and short-range order at interfaces modulate the activation energy of dislocation processes.
Changes in the activation energy of interface dislocation processes control the creep rate.
More coherent interfaces will produce lower creep rates than incoherent interfaces.
Chemically sharp interfaces will produce lower creep rates than intermixed interfaces.
The lower creep rate of coherent, sharp interfaces results from higher barriers to dislocation nucleation and transmission.
FCC/BCC HEA multilayers will have a significantly lower creep rate than single-phase HEA films of comparable composition and thickness.
Deformation will localize at or near the FCC/BCC interfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies when the FCC and BCC phases remain stable and test conditions do not cause phase instability or grain coarsening.
The proposed mechanism applies for interface spacings below approximately 100 nm.
At very small layer thicknesses, grain-boundary sliding or diffusion may contribute to creep.
